title: The Government That Sent Him to Paint This Later Hunted Him as a Communist
standfirst: In seven weeks in 1941, Cândido Portinari covered a Library of Congress hallway with ordinary sailors, his passage paid by an authoritarian Brazilian government and his invitation arranged through Nelson Rockefeller's wartime propaganda office. Four years later that same government banned his party and drove him into exile.

sections.heading: The Discovery Story Left Out Its Usual Cast
sections.body:
Discovery of the Land is the first of four panels Portinari painted for the vestibule outside the Library of Congress's Hispanic Reading Room, and its crowd is almost entirely deckhands. Reviewing the cycle at the time, the critic Robert C. Smith wrote that "violent excitement" runs through the composition and that "the symbol of the worker's hand is used in the most varied patterns." He went further on the brushwork itself: the men's features are abbreviated into gesture, noses reduced to hurried triangles, fingers left incomplete like notes struck and cut short.

A mural meant to dramatize the discovery of the Americas for Congress's own front hall had an obvious cast on hand — captains, viceroys, the priests of conquest. Portinari reached instead for the men hauling the rope, and never put a named explorer anywhere near the centre of the frame.

sections.heading: Seven Weeks of Wall, Two Governments, and a Fast Goodbye
sections.body:
The Library of Congress's Librarian, Archibald MacLeish, invited Portinari to paint the vestibule in 1940; Portinari reached Washington in June 1941 to start the work. He chose to paint straight onto dry plaster with tempera rather than wet fresco, believing it would "allow for a more brilliant blending of colors" and heighten the dramatic effect. A Brazilian magazine covering the job that year marvelled that "in seven weeks he painted more than 100 square meters of wall."

Brazil's government paid his passage to Washington. The invitation itself moved through the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs, the wartime agency Nelson Rockefeller ran to keep Latin America aligned with Washington rather than Berlin — even though Brazil hadn't picked a side yet. Getúlio Vargas didn't declare war on the Axis until 22 August 1942, seven months after the murals were inaugurated, and at home his government ran as "a federal presidential republic under an authoritarian corporatist dictatorship," complete with its own propaganda ministry. The murals were unveiled on 12 January 1942. Portinari wasn't there; he had already sailed for Brazil once the paint was down.

sections.heading: He Was Also the Rockefellers' Own Portraitist
sections.body:
The same Nelson Rockefeller running the wartime office that arranged the invitation also hired Portinari privately that year, commissioning a portrait of his wife, Mary Rockefeller, signed and dated 1941. The following year he commissioned a second, of his mother Abby Aldrich Rockefeller, a founding trustee of the Museum of Modern Art, where a Portinari canvas had already entered the collection in 1940. That second portrait was left unfinished for years: Abby Rockefeller died of a heart attack on 5 April 1948, and Portinari didn't complete her likeness until after her death.

The man overseeing hemispheric cultural diplomacy and the man painting his own family's faces were, for a stretch of the early 1940s, the same transaction.

sections.heading: Four Years Later, the Government That Sent Him Banned His Party
sections.body: Portinari joined the Brazilian Communist Party once the Estado Novo gave way to open elections, and in 1945 he ran for the Constituent Assembly on its slate. He lost, though the party itself elected the senator Luiz Carlos Prestes and fourteen deputies, among them the novelist Jorge Amado. Two years later he tried again, running for a Senate seat; early counts had him ahead, and he ultimately lost by a margin narrow enough that his own house museum's account says it "puts the honesty of the elections in check." That May, Brazil's Superior Electoral Court cancelled the Communist Party's registration outright and forced it underground.

sections.heading: He Left the Country Rather Than Wait to Be Arrested
sections.body: With the party banned and its members targeted, Portinari went into what his house museum's own record calls a "voluntary exile" in Uruguay. He didn't return until 1952, after a general amnesty let him back into Brazil. Washington, meanwhile, was no warmer: in 1949, at the height of the Red Scare, the United States denied him a visa to attend a peace conference, part of a stretch of roughly a dozen years in which McCarthyism kept him off the American art scene entirely — the same country that had flown him in on Rockefeller's own wartime office now shutting him out for the opposite politics.

sections.heading: He Finished a Monument to Peace While His Own Paint Was Poisoning Him
sections.body:
Brazil's government commissioned Portinari's last major work in the early 1950s: two panels for the United Nations, each roughly fourteen by ten metres, on the theme of War and Peace. He began studies in 1952 and finished the paintings in 1956, working the final stretch in nine months even though doctors had already warned him the lead in his pigments was poisoning him again. He pressed on anyway. Installed in 1957 in the delegates' lobby of the UN General Assembly Building, the panels drew a verdict from Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld: "the most important monumental work of art donated to the United Nations."

Portinari never saw them hang. His ties to the banned Communist Party kept him from the unveiling; the closest he came was watching the panels fully assembled at a Rio exhibition the year before they shipped. He died in Rio de Janeiro on 6 February 1962, while preparing for a show in Milan, poisoned by the same paints he had been mixing since Washington.
